sentences.text: Lukousaurus is an extinct archosauromorph known from a small snout with distinctive lacrimal horns found in Yunnan, China.
This animal possessed a robust skull for its size, and its teeth were initially thought to be typical of theropods.
Fossils including a partial skull, lower jaws, a tooth, and a humerus were discovered in the late 1930s in Huangchiatien, Yunnan Province.
The holotype skull was found in strata originally thought to be Triassic but are now known to be Early Jurassic.
The species name yini honors T. H. Yin, a former deputy director of the Geological Survey of China who worked during the Japanese invasion.
The holotype specimen is housed at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing under the number IVPP 23.
Lukousaurus was originally classified as a theropod dinosaur but later research suggests it may be related to suchian archosaurs.
Mickey Mortimer revised her classification of Lukousaurus from a ceratosaur or sphenosuchian to a basal pseudosuchian in 2011.
Studies by Knoll et al. (2012) and Irmis (2004) support the view that Lukousaurus is a suchian archosaur rather than a theropod or dinosauromorph.
Lukousaurus is classified within the suborder Loricata and infraorder Crocodylomorpha.
While long classified as a coelurosaurian theropod, Irmis (2004) and Knoll et al. (2012) classify Lukousaurus as a basal crocodylomorph.
Lukousaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 209 to 190 million years ago, in the Hettangian and Sinemurian stages.
The time range for Lukousaurus is estimated to be between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago.
The classification of Lukousaurus remains very uncertain due to the unusual characteristics of its type specimen and referred humerus.
